2023_002_m101723bdmtg.paragraph: Minutes of the Troy Board of Education regular meeting held October 17, 2023 at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois, called to order by President Schmidt at 7:00 p.m. and adjourned at 8:49 p.m. The Board adopted resolutions honoring sixty National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists and commemorating October 2023 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan, and approved the consent agenda and personnel recommendations. The most consequential action was acceptance of the District's audited 2023 financial statements, presented by Plante Moran audit partners Donna Hanson and Michael Walsh, who reported an unmodified opinion with no findings or questioned costs. Every recorded vote was 7 yes, 0 no.
2023_002_m101723bdmtg.page:
**Meeting**
Regular meeting of the Troy Board of Education, October 17, 2023, at the Troy School District Services Building, 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m.; the meeting adjourned at 8:49 p.m. Minutes signed by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary (notation GH/jh).

**Attendance**
Present with Mr. Schmidt: Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, and Wilson. Also present: Superintendent Machesky; administrators Montante, DiPilato, Pagel, Milanov, Zawislak, Brennan, Zawislak, Moynihan, and West; and Plante Moran audit partners Donna Hanson and Michael Walsh. Approximately 50 members of the audience attended.

**Recognition**
- TSD Mission Moment: Larson Middle School 7th grader Genevieve Kashat, one of 12 contestants in Kids Baking Championship Season 11, which premiered last December on the Food Network and Discovery+ channel. She has wanted to be a baker since she was 6 years old and runs a business on Instagram, @gens_kreations. Principal Brian Zawislak introduced her.
- Student Spotlight: Thomas Butcher, Troy School District Creative Content Producer, presented the October Creative Guild feature, recognizing Michelle Nartey, an Athens High School senior.

**Resolutions**

| Resolution | Moved / Supported | Vote |
| --- | --- | --- |
| National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists (sixty students) | Mrs. Alic / Mrs. Anne | Yes 7, No 0 |
| Learning Disabilities Month, October 2023 | Dr. Philippart / Dr. Wilson | Yes 7, No 0 |

More than one million students nationwide from some 21,000 high schools entered the National Merit Scholarship Program; approximately 16,000 seniors are selected as semifinalists, a status requiring scores in the top one and one-half percent on the PSAT and comparable scores on the SAT. Copies of the resolution will be presented at a reception on November 16th. The Learning Disabilities resolution notes that 1 in 5 individuals have a learning disability and joins Governor Gretchen Whitmer's declaration.

**Consent Agenda**
Moved by Mr. Hauff, supported by Mr. Haupt; items A through G approved 7-0: minutes of the September 5, 2023 Special Board of Education Meeting, Closed Session Meeting, and Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the September 19, 2023 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report - August 2023; TSD Bargaining Team; and Server Space Upgrade.

**Personnel**
Moved by Mr. Haupt, supported by Mrs. Alic, to approve the elementary and secondary personnel recommendations (Ashanti Daniels, Meredith Berlin). Yes 7, No 0.

**Business - 2022/2023 Audit**
Donna Hanson and Michael Walsh of Plante Moran presented the audit of the 2022-2023 fiscal year; a draft Audit Report had been presented in detail at the October 3, 2023 Board of Education Workshop. They reported an unmodified opinion with no findings or questioned costs in the 2023 financial statement and the 2023 federal program audit results, and discussed bond and sinking fund compliance, the non-recurring 147(c)(2) allocation, non-recurring revenue such as ESSER and childcare grants, the ASBO Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting for 2022, governmental funds, revenue and expenditures, student population, foundation allowance, and changes in federal funding. Board discussion covered ESSER and Hold Harmless funds and a budget still running very lean due to inflation despite funding increases. Finance Director Kandice Moynihan and Deputy Superintendent Rick West were recognized. Moved by Dr. Wilson, supported by Mrs. Alic, to accept and approve the audited 2023 financial statements. Yes 7, No 0.

**Public Communication**
Mrs. Michele Maleszyk, Troy resident and Barnard parent, addressed the ELA program and curriculum review program. Mrs. Tracy Owens, Troy resident and District parent, spoke on a resolution for Dyslexia Awareness Month and Learning Disabilities Awareness Month and on the Lucy Calkins, Fountas and Pinnell, and Reading Recovery programs.

**Other**
Student representative reports: Marlien William (Athens High School), Jayla Turner (Troy High School), Teagan Pruitt (Troy College and Career High School), Nurayda Albeez (International Academy-East). Board comments covered Manufacturing Day at Troy High, National Principal Appreciation Month, the new math curriculum, National Prescription Drug Take Back Day on Saturday, October 28th, Homecoming, Fall Updates to PTO/PTAs and staff on budget, enrollment, bond updates and Portrait of a Learner, and Smith Middle School planning. Upcoming: special meeting November 14th at 6:00 p.m. and Board Workshop at 7:00 p.m. in the Administration Building; December Workshop Tuesday, December 5th; regular meeting December 12th.
2023_002_m101723bdmtg.verbose:
Regular meeting minutes of the Board of Education, Troy, Michigan, for October 17, 2023, held at the Troy School District Services Building located at 4420 Livernois. President Schmidt called the meeting to order at 7:00 p.m. In addition to Mr. Schmidt, present were Board members Alic, Anne, Hauff, Haupt, Philippart, and Wilson. Also present were Superintendent Machesky and administrators Montante, DiPilato, Pagel, Milanov, Zawislak, Brennan, Zawislak, Moynihan, and West. Donna Hanson and Michael Walsh, audit partners from Plante Moran, were also in attendance. There were approximately 50 members of the audience. The minutes are respectfully submitted by Gary N. Hauff, Secretary, Troy Board of Education, and carry the notation GH/jh.

RECOGNITION - TSD MISSION MOMENT. The Board recognized Larson Middle School 7th grader Genevieve Kashat, one of 12 contestants who competed in the Kids Baking Championship Season 11, which premiered last December on the Food Network and Discovery+ channel. Genevieve has had the dream of being a baker since she was 6 years old and runs her own business on Instagram, @gens_kreations. The Board invited Principal Brian Zawislak to the podium to introduce Genevieve and ask her to share more about her television baking experience. Genevieve also treated Board members to a sample of her creations.

STUDENT SPOTLIGHT. The Board introduced Thomas Butcher, Troy School District Creative Content Producer, to share October's Student Spotlight, the monthly item of recognition in which students in the Creative Guild are featured to share their special accomplishments. The Board recognized Michelle Nartey, a senior at Athens High School; Thomas Butcher shared about her special talent in singing and songwriting.

NATIONAL MERIT SCHOLARSHIP SEMIFINALISTS. The minutes note that this year more than one million students nationwide, from some 21,000 high schools, entered the National Merit Scholarship Program, and that approximately 16,000 of these seniors are selected to be semifinalists. The Board commended and congratulated the District's sixty National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists: Rahim Basal, Vansh Baxi, Niveditha Chandrakanth, Michael Chen, Srivaishnavi Cherukuvada, Rahul Dandavolu, Vedant Das, Rohan Gajula-Ghosh, Kevin Hartwell, Mark Hong, Michael Hong, Jeffrey Hung, Karen Jin, Siddarth Karthikeyan, Mahee Kavdia, Lasya Kolli, Supratik Kuchibhatla, Claire Li, Steven Li, Brian Liu, Timothy Mathew, Brandon Mendoza, Sidharth Menon, Shreyas Mirle, Vishnu Nair, Anish Nandamuri, Sneha Nandwani, Huyen Nguyen, Nishit Palepu, Kush Parikh, Sruthi Pereddy, Sania Poonia, Ismail Qamar, Ashish Rajam, Ishanya Saini, Somya Sakalle, Akash Sarada, Aanya Shah, Akshaj Sharma, Karan Sharma, Sungat Shienh, Ashmit Shrivastava, Seongjin Shyn, Kanush Singh, Ananya Sri Raja Kalidindi, Nideesh Srivatsavan, Raghav Subramaniam, Jack Svoboda, Sanjay Tilak, Janhavi Tonge, Gautham Veettil, Eric Wong, Claire Wu, Julia Wu, Daniel Xiao, Yule Xie, Nathan Zerilli, Alan Zhang, Matthew Zhao, and Edison Zhou. The minutes call this a remarkable number of semifinalists and a tribute to the staff and parents of the Troy School District, and state that copies of the resolution will be presented to the students at a reception on November 16th.

The resolution, headed 2023 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists, was moved by Mrs. Alic and supported by Mrs. Anne. Its clauses recite that the sixty students earned the prestigious honor of being among those selected nationwide as this year's semifinalists; that student achievement is honored through the National Merit Scholarship semifinalist and finalist recognition programs; and that National Merit students reach semifinalist status by scoring in the top one and one-half percent on the National Preliminary Scholastic Aptitude Test (PSAT) and earning comparable scores on the Scholastic Aptitude Test (SAT). The Board adopted the resolution in honor of the students for their selection as 2024 National Merit Scholarship Semifinalists. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

LEARNING DISABILITIES AWARENESS MONTH. The minutes record that national associations for a number of different learning differences have each declared October as an awareness month, including associations for Dyslexia, Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder, and Down Syndrome, and that the U.S. Department of Education has declared October as Learning Disabilities / Dyslexia / Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder / Down Syndrome Awareness Month. In Michigan, Governor Whitmer has provided a more encompassing definition and declared October as Learning Disabilities Month, and the Troy Board of Education joined the governor with its own resolution.

The resolution was moved by Dr. Philippart and supported by Dr. Wilson. Its clauses state that the term learning disabilities refers to differences in how our brains work, which may affect the acquisition, organization, retention, understanding, or use of verbal or nonverbal information; that learning disabilities range in severity and may impact the acquisition and use of oral language, reading, written language, and mathematics; that 1 in 5 individuals have a learning disability; that learning disabilities may co-exist with other disabilities and conditions and can affect individuals regardless of race, gender, sexual orientation, or other intersecting factors; that disabilities are a natural part of human diversity but individuals with learning disabilities may face discrimination or marginalization; that every person has strengths and learning disabilities should not keep individuals from realizing their full potential; that specialized assessments and interventions involving home, school, community, and workplace settings can significantly enhance quality of life; and that understanding and celebrating the unique abilities of individuals with learning disabilities is essential to an inclusive society embracing the strengths and potential of all Michigan residents. The Board therefore joined Governor Gretchen Whitmer in commemorating October 2023 as Learning Disabilities Month in Michigan. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

ADDITIONS AND DELETIONS: None. PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (AGENDA ITEMS): None.

GENERAL - CONSENT AGENDA. It was moved by Mr. Hauff and supported by Mr. Haupt that the Troy Board of Education approve items A, B, C, D, E, F, and G on the consent agenda: minutes of the September 5, 2023 Special Board of Education Meeting; minutes of the September 5, 2023 Closed Session Meeting; minutes of the September 5, 2023 Board of Education Workshop; minutes of the September 19, 2023 Board of Education Meeting; Treasurer's Report - August 2023; TSD Bargaining Team; and Server Space Upgrade. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

PERSONNEL - ELEMENTARY AND SECONDARY. It was moved by Mr. Haupt and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Board of Education approve the personnel recommendations as stated, naming Ashanti Daniels and Meredith Berlin. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

CURRICULUM: None.

BUSINESS - 2022/2023 AUDIT REPORT. Ms. Donna Hanson and Mr. Michael Walsh, audit partners from Plante Moran, provided a presentation to the Board of Education on the audit of the 2022-2023 fiscal year. A draft copy of the District's Audit Report had been presented in detail to the Board at the October 3, 2023 Board of Education Workshop. Ms. Hanson and Mr. Walsh provided highlights of the audit and were pleased to share the results of an unmodified opinion with no findings or questioned costs in the 2023 financial statement and the 2023 federal program audit results. They spoke about bond and sinking fund compliance, the non-recurring 147(c)(2) allocation, non-recurring funding sources of revenue such as ESSER and childcare grants, and the ASBO Certificate of Excellence in Financial Reporting for 2022. Governmental funds, revenue and expenditures were also reviewed along with student population, foundation allowance, and changes in federal funding. There was discussion among Board members regarding the ESSER and Hold Harmless funds and how the budget is still running very lean due to inflation even with the increases in funding. The audit partners and Board members recognized the Business Office staff, Finance Director Kandice Moynihan, and Rick West, Deputy Superintendent, for their exceptional work in managing the budget.

2022/2023 AUDIT ACTION. It was moved by Dr. Wilson and supported by Mrs. Alic that the Board of Education accept and approve the Troy School District's audited 2023 financial statements as presented by Plante Moran. The vote was Yes 7, No 0.

PUBLIC COMMUNICATION (NON-AGENDA ITEMS). Mrs. Michele Maleszyk, Troy resident and parent of a Barnard student, addressed the Board about the current ELA program and curriculum review program. Mrs. Tracy Owens, Troy resident and parent in the District, addressed the Board about a resolution for Dyslexia Awareness Month and Learning Disabilities Awareness Month; she also spoke about the Lucy Calkins, Fountas and Pinnell, and Reading Recovery Program and asked the Board to embrace the changes the state is making regarding literature.

OTHER: None recorded under that heading.

REPORTS FROM STUDENT REPRESENTATIVES TO THE BOARD. Marlien William, student representative for Athens High School, shared a report on events and activities at Athens. Jayla Turner, student representative for Troy High School, reported on events and activities at Troy High. Teagan Pruitt, student representative for Troy College and Career High School, reported on events and activities at TCCHS. Nurayda Albeez, student representative for International Academy-East, reported on events and activities at IAE.

BOARD MEMBER COMMENTS. Dr. Philippart mentioned how wonderful it was to hear about Genevieve's and Michelle's accomplishments and about the events giving students opportunities to be involved. Mr. Haupt talked about his visit to Troy High School for Manufacturing Day and the opportunities the program will bring for students in engineering and manufacturing fields, and recognized principals for National Principal Appreciation Month. Mrs. Alic talked about the new math curriculum and how engaged students were when she visited 5th and 8th grade classrooms. Mr. Hauff announced that Saturday, October 28th is National Prescription Drug Take Back Day, when community members can dispose of unused or expired medications by putting them in a baggie and dropping them off in the lobby of the police department. Dr. Wilson talked about how great Homecoming was for both high schools, expressed gratitude for the principals, and mentioned the upcoming fall plays at the high school theatres. Dr. Machesky announced that the Central Office team has begun to present Fall Updates to PTO/PTAs and TSD staff covering budget, enrollment, bond updates, and Portrait of a Learner; he thanked the community for supporting the Bond initiative and discussed the timeline for bond projects. Mr. Schmidt talked about the new Smith Middle School planning process and about a classroom visit to see MTSS in action, noting that 8th grade students owned their learning and that their enthusiasm was palpable.

UPCOMING MEETINGS. Mr. Schmidt announced that a special meeting will be held on November 14th at 6:00 p.m., followed by the Board Workshop beginning at 7:00 p.m. in the Administration Building. The December Workshop will be held on Tuesday, December 5th, and the regular meeting will be held on December 12th.

ADJOURNMENT. The meeting adjourned at 8:49 p.m.

2023_003_gold_medallion_judge_feedback_t.paragraph: Judge feedback from the 2023 Gold Medallion Awards for the Troy School District, scoring the district's bond communications campaign entry across four weighted categories and summarizing narrative comments from the review panel. Category scores were Research 4.83/5.00, Planning 4.67/5.00, Implementation 4.67/5.00, Evaluation 4.50/5.00, and Overall 4.67/5.00, against an MSPRA threshold requiring a weighted average of 4.50/5.00, or 90%, to receive the award. Judges repeatedly urged tighter linkage of goals, objectives, strategies, and tactics, and several recommended the entry be submitted for an NSPRA Gold Medallion as well.
2023_003_gold_medallion_judge_feedback_t.page:
**Award and scoring**
2023 Gold Medallion Awards judge feedback for Troy School District, issued by MSPRA. Each category is scored on a scale of 1.00 to 5.00, and entries must receive a weighted average of 4.50/5.00, or 90%, to receive the award. Judging is done confidentially by an experienced panel of accredited state and national association members and public relations professionals, who provide constructive feedback for all entries.

| Category | Score | Weight |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Research | 4.83/5.00 | 15% of the score |
| Planning | 4.67/5.00 | 45% of the score |
| Implementation | 4.67/5.00 | 25% of the score |
| Evaluation | 4.50/5.00 | 15% of the score |
| Overall | 4.67/5.00 | - |

**Research comments**
Judges called the section very thorough, praised survey feedback on building needs as necessary primary research, and noted objectives were SMART and aligned with research. Suggestions: add charts and graphs from the community survey for visual variety; compare community survey results with community voting demographics; explicitly label the project goal even if identical to the district goal; tighten the third objective, which one judge said should end at motivating families and staff to vote; and identify which items were primary versus secondary and formal versus informal, plus the specific research methodologies used.

**Planning comments**
Judges described a very detailed plan with set roles, objectives, strategies, and tactics, and commended the environmental scan, the identification of target audiences, the inclusion of the budget and team roles and responsibilities, and the tie to the district strategic plan. One judge highlighted the entry's statement that it was crucial to be flexible and able to adapt to changing conditions. Recommendations: attribute some material (political climate, board election campaigns and results, economics) to research; consider whether the Concurrent Campaign section belongs under evaluation; detail each strategy and tactic and tie each to an objective; and outline the five planning elements - goals, public identification, objectives naming the target public for each strategy, SMART objectives, and defined strategies and tactics.

**Implementation comments**
Judges praised key messages drawn from survey research, clear targeting through research-proven outlets, the real estate agent video promoting district value, visually appealing graphics and branding, per-campus adjustments on flyers, newspaper insert and PowerPoint slides, the introductory video, the principal toolkit, the FAQ, and timeline execution. Noted issues: automatic captions on videos should be reviewed and corrected to meet web accessibility standards; one judge could not access the principal toolkit without login information; and details on specific messages and channels against the timeline, budget, and responsible party would strengthen the section.

**Evaluation comments**
Follow-up interviews to determine messaging effectiveness were cited as strong primary research. Judges recommended returning to each element of GOST (Goals, Objectives, Strategies, Tactics) with supporting data for each strategy - newsletter open rates, social media engagement, website views, video watch time - and sharing specifics on the success of individual objectives, including whether objectives were outcome- or output-based and whether awareness, opinions, behavior, or support changed.

**Overall comments and criteria**
Judges liked the entry's focus on the communications campaign rather than the creation of the bond projects, valued the hyperlinks to additional information, and asked for more on how absentee voters were reached. Two judges recommended submitting the campaign for an NSPRA Gold Medallion. Overall criteria: the project is based in strategic communication best practices; the concept is clear and the writing is free of errors; the content is well-organized, visually appealing, and appropriate; the program, school, and/or district brand is portrayed consistently; and the project fulfills the stated objectives and goals.
2023_003_gold_medallion_judge_feedback_t.verbose:
The 2023 Gold Medallion Awards judge feedback report for Troy School District records category scores and anonymous panel commentary on the district's bond communications campaign entry. Scores were Research 4.83/5.00, Planning 4.67/5.00, Implementation 4.67/5.00, Evaluation 4.50/5.00, and Overall 4.67/5.00.

RESEARCH (4.83/5.00). One judge called the section very thorough, covering a variety of aspects of the program and types of research conducted, and said the survey feedback on building needs provided necessary primary research, that objectives are in line with the research and are SMART, and that the entry touched on how research and evaluation continued to impact planning and implementation throughout the project. That judge recommended, if the campaign is submitted in other award programs, adding charts and graphs from the community survey to provide visual variety and turn numbers into easy-to-read points, and adding something about the voting demographics of the community and whether the community survey results aligned with those numbers. A second judge praised the detailing of research used to inform decision-making, said it helped tell the story and provide the rationale for the project, and called the variety of data used and cited - both primary and secondary - impressive and appreciated; that judge suggested specifically stating and calling out the goal or goals, noting it can be the exact same as the district goal but should also be labeled as the goal for the project or plan, and suggested tightening the third objective, observing that the first and second detail what is being attempted, by how much, and when, while the third is wordier and loses focus, with much of it better placed as a strategy (how the objective will be carried out) or as a tactic (the tools used to execute a strategy). Other comments: fantastic research reaching all stakeholders and outside assessments; great research, but the third objective is too broad and starts to get into strategies and tactics and should end at motivating families and staff to vote; research could be stronger if the entry had included what items were primary and secondary, formal and informal, and the specific research methodologies used; and the entry demonstrates excellent research and outlines goals and objectives that align to research findings.

PLANNING (4.67/5.00). One judge felt some information in the section could also be attributed to research (political climate, board election campaigns and results, economics) and asked whether the Concurrent Campaign section could be considered part of the evaluation, noting that incorporating additional information to explain actions helps show decisions are informed by research. Another judge commended the identification and detailing of target audiences and specifically appreciated the entry's statement that it was crucial to be flexible and be able to adapt to changing conditions as they developed, calling that a hallmark of a public relations professional. That judge also appreciated that the scope of work was considered and categorized in a way target audiences could more easily understand and remember, praised the completion of an environmental scan and its inclusion in the plan and award submission, and again credited masterful use of research and data to inform decision-making. For future submissions the judge encouraged detailing each strategy and tactic, explaining that strategies detail how objectives will be carried out and each strategy needs to be tied to an objective - for example, if an objective is to increase community awareness in low voter turnout areas by a given percentage by a given date, a strategy could be advertising in targeted neighborhoods, with tactics such as yard signs and billboards - and noted that doing so helps assess whether the plan was successfully implemented and whether it had the desired impact. The judge thanked the district for completing and including its budget and team roles and responsibilities. Additional comments: a very detailed plan with set roles, objectives, strategies and tactics; excellent, with a good job tying the campaign into the strategic plan; planning could only be improved by specifically outlining the five planning elements that provide the framework for all communication plans - goals; public identification to establish clearly defined groups; objectives that indicate the target public for each outlined strategy; SMART objectives; and defined strategies (the how) and tactics (the what); and the entry demonstrates a sophisticated and thorough grasp of planning, reflecting a clear understanding of target audiences and communications tactics.

IMPLEMENTATION (4.67/5.00). Judges noted that research from the initial survey feedback and the community survey showed phrases and needs that resonated with stakeholders and were turned into key messages, and that messages were clear and targeted to appropriate audiences through research-proven outlets; one judge singled out the idea of having a real estate agent create a video to promote the value of the district. Another judge called the graphics visually appealing and attention-grabbing with well-done branding, calling out the adjustments made for each campus on the flyers, newspaper insert, and PowerPoint slides, and describing the language as clear, concise, and appropriate and the videos as great, with the introductory video setting a good tone for the campaign ahead. That judge asked that all materials meet web accessibility standards, specifically reviewing and correcting the automatic captions on videos, so materials are readily available to all audiences; called the principal toolkit a wonderful idea while noting the judge could not access it because login information was required; praised the key messages and the willingness to adjust them throughout the campaign; described the FAQ as well-organized and easy to navigate; and commended the timeline execution. Other comments: beautiful campaign; well-designed graphics and consistent use throughout the campaign; implementation could be improved by including details on the specific messages and channels against the timeline, budget, and designated responsible party, which is also the time to monitor results of actions and messages while tracking campaign milestones; and the campaign was successfully implemented, producing materials of a high quality that supported stated goals in accordance with a clear timeline.

EVALUATION (4.50/5.00). Judges called the evaluation thorough and cited follow-up interviews to determine the effectiveness of messaging and how information was shown as a great example of primary research and as information usable for future campaigns. One judge congratulated the district on a successful campaign and on following up with members of target audiences to understand which tactics were most successful, praised the detailing of next steps and called the tactics visually appealing, easy to read, and key to the campaign's success; that judge advised going back to each element of GOST (Goals, Objectives, Strategies, Tactics) to determine whether the district met or exceeded what it set out to do, including data for each strategy such as newsletter analytics (open rate), social media (engagement), website (views), and videos (watch time), and noted that much of that framework already appears in subsequent pages of the award submission. Additional comments: congratulations on the win and great evaluation; love the data points and the detail, with a good job tying evaluation back to goals and objectives; evaluation could only be improved by sharing specifics on the success of individual objectives, asking whether objectives were outcome- or output-based and whether there was a change in awareness, opinions, behavior, or support for the outlined goal, and identifying ways to improve and recommendations for the future; and it seems clear the campaign achieved its objectives, with follow-up interviews bringing specificity and clarity to what might otherwise have been difficult to measure.

OVERALL (4.67/5.00). One judge liked that the entry focused on the communications campaign rather than the creation of the bond projects, called the quality of materials high, suggested adding more about how absentee voters were reached and what messaging they received, and - anticipating an NSPRA Gold Medallion entry - recommended having a few editors review and clean it up. Another thanked the district for including hyperlinks to additional information, said it made for an even more thorough submission, urged that tactics be tied to strategies, objectives, and goals so impact can be directly demonstrated and measured, and called the campaign inspiring. Other overall comments: great job; this is a great campaign, please consider submitting it for an NSPRA Gold Medallion as well; overall this is a strong submission; and excellent work.

RUBRIC. MSPRA uses an experienced panel of accredited state and national association members and public relations professionals to confidentially review and judge entries, and judges provide constructive feedback for all entries. Each category is scored on a scale of 1.00 to 5.00, and entries must receive a weighted average of 4.50/5.00, or 90%, to receive the award. Overall criteria considered when reviewing the entry in its entirety: the project is based in strategic communication best practices; the concept is clear and the writing is free of errors; the content is well-organized, visually appealing, and appropriate; the program, school, and/or district brand is portrayed consistently; and the project fulfills the stated objectives and goals.

Research counts for 15% of the score, and judges ask whether the reason for the project is explained, whether there is evidence of quality and varied methods of research performed, whether findings were used to guide planning, and whether project goals and measurable objectives are stated. Planning counts for 45% of the score, with judges asking whether target audiences were identified, whether strategies were determined for accomplishing objectives, what stakeholders were involved in the planning process, whether a variety of communication tactics were proposed to reach target audiences, what relevant training was provided for key staff, whether a communications budget was developed, and whether team roles and responsibilities were identified. Implementation counts for 25% of the score, with judges asking whether the team created a timeline and met key dates, whether planned strategies and tactics were implemented, what key messages were used to support the goals and objectives, whether audience response was monitored, whether the design of materials was visually appealing, and whether appropriate and clear language was used. Evaluation counts for 15% of the score, with judges asking whether the project was successful based on the goals and objectives, what indicators were used to measure success, whether specific data was collected on the effectiveness of specific strategies and tactics, whether opportunities for improvement were explored for future projects, and what next steps were identified.

2023_004_excellence_awards_judge_feedbac.paragraph: Judge feedback from the 2023 Excellence Awards for Troy School District, compiling panel comments on strengths and recommended improvements for entries in seven categories: Audio/Podcast, Financial Report, Marketing Materials, Newsletter, Social Media, Video, and Website/Mobile App. No numeric scores are reported; instead the report pairs narrative praise with specific criticism, most of it recurring around volume of content, accessibility, and readability. The document closes with the judging rubric, listing the elements considered for all categories plus category-specific criteria, including the requirement that Website/Mobile App content and design be accessible for all users under WCAG 2.1 Level AA.
2023_004_excellence_awards_judge_feedbac.page:
**Report**
2023 Excellence Awards judge feedback for Troy School District. Each category section lists what judges considered the strengths of the entry and what recommendations they had for improving it. No scores are printed.

**Audio/Podcast**
Strengths: tying past and present under the district's overall legacy; strong interviews and editing; innovative and compelling celebration of a district milestone using storytelling as a window to the past; exceptional storytelling and quality audio. Recommendations: add context near the start for listeners less familiar with district history, and open with a brief word from the team explaining the context of the 1989 Athens State Soccer Championship and its relevance today.

**Financial Report**
Strengths: thorough document offering a wealth of information for voters; multiple points of view (students, board president, Realtor); content broken into small, concise chunks; colorful design; comprehensive overview of Troy's bond issue with images of infrastructure clearly in need of repair. Recommendations: shorten the newsletter or add an index or table of contents; use more bullet points; apply more consistent capitalization, type sizes, and typefaces; make the colors for the four areas of the plan consistent throughout, since it was challenging to track improvements by area and grade level or building.

**Marketing Materials**
Strengths: at-a-glance information, visually appealing and unique to each school's colors; consistency across schools with nice infographics; the Hamilton Elementary homepage with a drone video progressing into Hamilton at a glance and the five-star rating from Troy community parents and students. Recommendations: combine the busy school and district mission sections; check ADA accessibility; replace links showing NEW MISSION INFOGRAPHIC COMING SOON with a placeholder graphic; allow more white space.

**Newsletter**
Strengths: consistent message and appearance; front page of each issue clearly identifies the district; contributions from both superintendent and board president; the roundup on the last page; wide variety of topics and programs with numerous pictures and clear branding. Recommendations: balance photos and text; make recurring content consistent between issues (athlete signings differed each issue); reduce excessive graphics; address low-resolution elements; increase font size; add contact information and ways to stay connected.

**Social Media**
Strengths: consistency across campaign-related posts; use of historical video; simple, clear messages; quick facts and footage. Recommendations: better engage the interactive social functions of social media, and include the date of the vote in videos to direct the audience to take action.

**Video**
Strengths: classroom footage; graphics and an attention-getting opening; natural sound; professional footage with excellent b-roll; the sixth grade teacher's segments; an explainer style suited to answering community questions, with easy-to-read flowcharts illustrating math course sequences. Recommendations: shorten the video and reduce educational jargon; interview the math specialist somewhere other than what looked like a living room; avoid closed captioning covering graphics; simplify the student track graphics; add a clear summary structure connecting the changes to student benefit; reconsider the all-caps title cards with tight bounding boxes, including text such as the one at 4:40.

**Website/Mobile App**
Strengths: a collective location for press-related content, including both press releases and a media coverage area; convenient aggregation of news regardless of outlet; a button for visitors to submit news and story ideas; simple, easy navigation and a good mobile version. Recommendations: the press release module is not mobile-friendly; the media coverage page's last column gets cut off even on a full-screen desktop; rework the media logos without the blue boxes and link to their homepages; add a link back to the main Press Room page; note that the media spreadsheet may be hard to keep updated as media links change, and confirm PDF newsletters are ADA-compliant.

**Rubric**
Elements considered for all categories: purpose and target audience well defined or implied; clear, concise, positive writing; text free of grammatical, spelling, and punctuation errors; well-organized, visually appealing, appropriate content; and consistent portrayal of the program, school, and/or district brand. Additional criteria are listed for Annual Report, Audio/Podcast, Diversity Equity and Inclusion, Financial Report, Marketing Materials, Newsletter, Special Purpose, Video, Social Media, and Website/Mobile App, the last requiring accessibility for all users at WCAG 2.1 Level AA.
2023_004_excellence_awards_judge_feedbac.verbose:
The 2023 Excellence Awards judge feedback report for Troy School District collects panel comments on the district's entries, organized by category, with each category divided into what judges considered the strengths of the entry and what recommendations they had for improving it. The categories addressed are Audio/Podcast, Financial Report, Marketing Materials, Newsletter, Social Media, Video, and Website/Mobile App. The report contains no numeric scores.

AUDIO/PODCAST. Strengths cited: a really exciting way to tie in the past and the present under the district's overall legacy in this area, with a great job on the interviews and editing; an innovative and compelling way to celebrate a district milestone using storytelling as a window to the past that also connects the community to today; a judge who really enjoyed the submission and called it a great podcast from start to finish; and exceptional storytelling with quality audio. Recommendations: some additional context near the start would help listeners who are not as familiar with the district history, and many listeners might appreciate a brief word from the team introducing the episode so all listeners better understand the context of the 1989 Athens State Soccer Championship and why it is relevant to today.

FINANCIAL REPORT. Strengths cited: the document appears very thorough and offers a wealth of information for voters, includes a variety of points of view (students, board president, Realtor), breaks content into small, concise chunks, and has a colorful, eye-catching design; it is a very comprehensive overview of Troy's bond issue, providing many examples of what could be in Troy's future and including images of infrastructure clearly in need of repair; it is very detailed in explaining every component of the Bond, which is important to some audiences; and it is visually appealing with creative use of information formatting. Recommendations: either making the newsletter shorter with fewer pages or providing an index or table of contents could have improved the entry, because the volume of information presented without a clear road map could be overwhelming, and more consistent use of capitalization, type sizes, and typefaces could have enhanced the professional appearance; there is a lot of text and bullet points would make it more engaging and easier to digest; and the colors for the four areas of the plan were not consistent throughout, with one judge doubting the average person would read so much content and finding it challenging to keep track of all the improvements by area and grade level or building, while recognizing that it was a financial supplement.

MARKETING MATERIALS. Strengths cited: the at-a-glance information, visually appealing and unique to each school's colors; consistency across the various individual schools with nice infographics and great content; the Hamilton Elementary homepage, described as engaging, with the movement of the drone video up top progressing into Hamilton at a glance, showcasing positive aspects and community feedback such as the five-star rating from Troy community parents and students; and materials that are very well organized and consistent across all schools, inviting, easy to read, and colorful. Recommendations: one judge found the first two sections with the school and District's missions busy and would like them combined, since each school's mission should still fit within the District's overall goal, arguing a cleaner, more streamlined design would push people to read the text rather than skim over it; another worried about how accessible (ADA) the materials are on the website; another reported that clicking some submission links produced a page reading NEW MISSION INFOGRAPHIC COMING SOON and found the graphic design a little overwhelming, noting the brain needs white space to process; and a judge recommended a placeholder graphic for the missing Mission Statement graphic that is currently empty.

NEWSLETTER. Strengths cited: consistency with the message and with the appearance; front pages that make clear the publication comes from the district; coverage of many topics with contributions from both the superintendent and the board president and a roundup on the last page; a wide variety of topics and programs that make it a great community resource; and numerous pictures that enhanced the reading experience, with clear and noticeable branding. Recommendations: in some cases additional photos would help tell the story while in others there are too many photos and not enough text; some pages are very busy and difficult to read because the reader does not know where to focus, and more consistency between issues in how the same type of information is shared would help, with the athlete signings standing out as very different in each issue; the amount of content is a little overwhelming and the extra graphics a little excessive; consider a less-is-more approach, since the many visual elements can be a tad distracting and some graphic elements are strained due to lower resolution than their surrounding elements; and to enhance readability consider increasing the font size and adding contact information or promoting ways to stay connected with the district.

SOCIAL MEDIA. Strengths cited: consistency across campaign-related posts and the use of historical video; the use of video to engage and inform the community; simple, clear messages that are easy to consume; and a highly enjoyed submission with quick facts and footage. Recommendations: aside from information distribution, consider how to better engage the social functions and interaction of social media; one judge offered no recommendations, acknowledging how hard a bond campaign is; and the videos did not include the date of the vote, which would have helped direct the audience to take action.

VIDEO. Strengths cited: good shots of kids doing work in the classroom; nice graphics with an opening that immediately caught a judge's attention and good use of natural sound such as a teacher giving instructions; professional-looking footage with excellent b-roll and great messaging; a sixth grade teacher described as awesome who seems to encompass the whole program in her segments, along with video of her interacting with students; and a slightly longer explainer style that fits the purpose of answering community questions, with solid audio and video quality, classroom footage framed well in a variety of angles that keep it from feeling repetitive, easy-to-read flowcharts illustrating the math course sequences, and speakers and footage fitting together into a very cohesive video. Recommendations: the video was really long and contained quite a bit of educational jargon; one judge would have interviewed the math specialist and a few others in a different location because it looked like a living room, found some speakers too rehearsed, and thought the video too long to hold attention; another suggested shortening it, noted graphics can be difficult to read while listening to the narrator, and observed that closed captioning covers graphics; another suggested making more of preparing students for the future, noted the background sign reading show me what you are thinking might have made a nice b-roll piece, and found the graphics showing student track too busy for video; and a final judge said each speaker communicates well and the individual changes and reasoning behind them are mentioned, but would have liked a clear summary or video structure to connect the dots - observing a situation, investigating all parts of the math program, and implementing specific changes with an explanation of how each helps students - adding that the all-caps title cards with tight bounding boxes look phenomenal visually but are uncomfortable to read and that some of their text, such as at 4:40, could be more succinct or punctuated differently.

WEBSITE/MOBILE APP. Strengths cited: a collective location for press-related content is an excellent idea for a school district, with appreciation for both the press release section and the media coverage area; aggregating all news content in one area makes it convenient for users to find what they want regardless of outlet, with a judge speculating that the Media Coverage page populates automatically and calling that super cool, and praising the button for visitors to submit news and story ideas; the simplicity of the page, which is easy to navigate, makes its exact purpose easy to tell, requires no searching or multiple click-throughs, and has a mobile version that looks great; and a page that is easy to view without too much going on. Recommendations: one judge encountered many issues accessing content on a phone, finding that while the page itself was responsive the content was not, requiring side-to-side scrolling inside the page to reach articles and links; another noted the module that displays press releases is not mobile-friendly and that updating it would be a big improvement, suggested changes to the media coverage page because the last column does not quite fit the view and gets cut off even on a full-screen desktop, proposed a different look for the media logos without the blue boxes with links to their homepages from what appear to be buttons at the bottom of the page, and asked for a link back to the main Press Room page from all linked pages; another thought the media spreadsheet will be difficult to keep updated in the long run because links on media sites often change or do not last, found the newsletter a little slow to load and harder to navigate, and questioned whether a PDF format is ADA-compliant and accessible to all audiences; and a final recommendation was to include a document with the audience and purpose behind the page.

RUBRIC. Elements considered by judges for entries in all categories: the purpose and target audience are well defined or implied; the writing is clear, concise, and positive; the text is free of grammatical, spelling, and punctuation errors; the content is well-organized, visually appealing, and appropriate; and the program, school, and/or district brand is portrayed consistently. Additional elements are listed by category. Annual Report, Special Purpose, and Financial Report share the requirements that font and graphic elements be easy to read and enhance the overall design and that there be an effective balance of written and visual information; Annual Report and Special Purpose add that format and length be appropriate for the content and target audiences, while Financial Report adds that complicated topics be made relevant and easy to understand for the target audiences. Audio/Podcast: editing is smooth, organized, and well-paced; topics are engaging, innovative, and relevant; narration, music, and other sounds are of good and consistent quality. Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion: the project is intentionally designed to positively impact, support, or promote DEI efforts; its message and voice are appropriate, approachable, and engaging; and multiple perspectives were considered and consulted. Marketing Materials: the program, school, or district is presented in a creative, persuasive, and positive way; font and graphic elements are easy to read; and there is a compelling call to action. Newsletter: topics are varied and engaging; font and graphic elements are easy to read; and consistency is shown across multiple issues. Video, listed twice in the rubric with identical criteria: editing is smooth, organized, and well-paced; the video includes closed captioning; and video, narration, still photos, music, and graphics are integrated effectively and consistently. Social Media: posts include a high-quality photo, graphic, or video; audience engagement is apparent and encouraged; and posts reflect platform best practices related to accessibility, frequency, style, and voice. Website/Mobile App: user navigation is intuitive and responsive on a mobile device; content appears current and regularly updated; and the content and design are accessible for all users (WCAG 2.1 Level AA).
